grounded_facts: The final item removed from the box is a bound stack of manuscript pages, which begins with a note from Watson explaining the confidential nature of the unpublished cases.
memories.memory_text: I recall removing the final item from my dispatch box—a bound manuscript—and beginning to read the note I had written, explaining how certain cases were withheld for their delicate and scandalous nature, not to be revealed until long after my death.

grounded_facts: Watson leaves a written message explaining his decision to withhold certain cases from publication during his lifetime.
memories.memory_text: I left a written message stating that the box should not be opened until fifty years after my death, and I made clear my decision to withhold some cases during my lifetime due to discretion.

grounded_facts: Holmes and Watson arrive at 221B Baker Street by hansom cab, marking the beginning of their residence there.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Holmes and Watson arrive at 221B Baker Street by hansom cab, marking the beginning of their residence there.

grounded_facts: Holmes and Watson return to their residence at 221B Baker Street after a journey, greeted by Mrs. Hudson.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Holmes and Watson return to their residence at 221B Baker Street after a journey, greeted by Mrs. Hudson.

grounded_facts: Mrs. Hudson warmly greets Holmes and Watson upon their arrival at 221B Baker Street.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Mrs. Hudson warmly greets Holmes and Watson upon their arrival at 221B Baker Street.

grounded_facts: Holmes and Watson arrive back at 221B Baker Street, reestablishing the familiar setting and routine.
memories.memory_text: I arrived back at 221B Baker Street with Holmes, took off my hat and coat, and set my medical bag down just as the cabbie left.

grounded_facts: Holmes accuses Watson of romanticizing and exaggerating his character in published stories.
memories.memory_text: Holmes confronted me, saying I romanticized and exaggerated him in my stories—he told me I made him six-foot-four instead of six-foot-one, gave him an improbable costume, portrayed him as a violin virtuoso when he says he's barely competent, and painted him as a misogynist when he claims he merely distrusts women because of the 'twinkle in the eye and the arsenic in the soup.'

grounded_facts: Holmes dismisses the case of the missing Tumbling Piccolos, deeming the reward too low and the matter likely trivial.
memories.memory_text: I was present when Holmes dismissed the case of the missing Tumbling Piccolos, saying the circus owner offered only five pounds — less than a pound per midget — and that the little fellows had likely run off to join another circus.

grounded_facts: Holmes discovers that something crucial is missing from his desk, which he attributes to Mrs. Hudson's cleaning against his orders.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes notice something missing from his desk and accuse Mrs. Hudson of tidying against his orders, saying something very crucial was gone.

grounded_facts: Holmes explains that dust on his desk is part of his document dating system, justifying his anger at her cleaning.
memories.memory_text: I heard Holmes explain to Mrs. Hudson that the dust on his desk is part of his filing system, allowing him to date documents by its thickness.

grounded_facts: Watson explains and justifies Holmes's tobacco ash experiment to Mrs. Hudson, who is critical of the smoky conditions.
memories.memory_text: I explained to Mrs. Hudson that Holmes was working on a definitive study of tobacco ash to justify the smoky conditions she objected to.

grounded_facts: Holmes tells Watson he envies his calm and untroubled mind, contrasting it with his own restless intellect.
memories.memory_text: Holmes told me he envies my calm and untroubled mind, saying it's placid and prosaic, while his own mind rebels against stagnation like a racing engine tearing itself apart from lack of work.

grounded_facts: Watson challenges Holmes's decision to use cocaine, questioning his self-control and expressing shame.
memories.memory_text: I confronted Holmes, calling out to him and asking where his self-control was, and I told him he should be ashamed of himself for what he was doing.

grounded_facts: Holmes conducts a scientific experiment involving the combustion and analysis of various tobacco products to study their ash residues.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes conducting his experiment with tobacco, carefully studying the ash under a microscope, and I remember him saying it would take care of it thoroughly.

grounded_facts: Holmes, feeling mentally stagnant and unchallenged, decides to inject himself with cocaine as a means of coping with his inner restlessness.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes take my medical bag, pull out the cocaine, and start preparing to inject himself—rolling up his sleeve, getting the syringe—so I inferred he must be feeling mentally stagnant and using the drug to cope with that restlessness.

grounded_facts: Watson claims Holmes only lives with him to access stimulants, challenging the integrity of their relationship.
memories.memory_text: I told Holmes the only reason he moved in with me was to have a steady supply of stimulants, and I could see it struck a nerve.

grounded_facts: Upon Mrs. Hudson's entrance, Holmes conceals the hypodermic syringe behind his back, indicating shame or desire to hide his drug use.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes quickly hide the hypodermic behind his back the moment Mrs. Hudson walked in, as if he were ashamed of being caught with it.

grounded_facts: Holmes tells Watson where he hid his medical bag, demonstrating familiarity and observation.
memories.memory_text: I was looking for my medical bag, and Holmes told me I had hidden it under the Moorish table.

grounded_facts: Watson announces his decision to leave 221B Baker Street and resume his medical practice, marking a significant shift in his living arrangement and relationship with Holmes.
memories.memory_text: I announced to Mrs. Hudson and then to Holmes that I'm moving out, and I made sure to tell Holmes I'll keep paying my half of the rent until he finds someone else to share the rooms.

grounded_facts: Watson provides Holmes with a new hypodermic needle and leaves behind three bottles of narcotics, symbolizing both care and resignation regarding Holmes's addiction.
memories.memory_text: I gave Holmes a fresh hypodermic needle and left three bottles of narcotics on the mantel as my farewell gift, knowing it was both an act of care and an acceptance that I could no longer stop his addiction.

grounded_facts: Watson states he won't watch Holmes destroy himself with drugs, asserting personal boundaries.
memories.memory_text: I told Holmes that if he wanted to destroy himself with drugs, he could go ahead—but I made it clear I wouldn't stay and watch it happen.

grounded_facts: A heated argument between Watson and Holmes about Holmes's drug use and living situation, culminating in Watson's announcement to move out.
memories.memory_text: I remember the rain outside and how the argument with Holmes escalated—when he pulled out the hypodermic, I glared, and when Mrs. Hudson walked in, he hid it. I kept my composure, searched the room for my things, and later handed him a fresh needle as a farewell gesture, though he only said my name in response.

grounded_facts: A structured moment in which Watson packs and prepares to leave 221B Baker Street, marking a significant personal and narrative transition.
Watson begins packing his belongings, indicating his intention to move out of the shared residence with Holmes.
memories.memory_text: I was packing my belongings at 221B Baker Street, moving around the room with open valises, preparing to leave the place I'd shared with Holmes.

grounded_facts: Watson dismisses Mrs. Hudson's emotional display, signaling his determination to move on.
memories.memory_text: I told Mrs. Hudson not to make a fuss when she started expressing her sorrow, because I needed to stay firm about my decision to move on.

grounded_facts: Watson informs Mrs. Hudson of his temporary lodging at Brown's Hotel.
memories.memory_text: I let Mrs. Hudson know I'd be staying at Brown's Hotel for the time being, so she could reach me if needed.

grounded_facts: Mrs. Hudson expresses sorrow over Watson's departure and references her own past emotional trauma.
memories.memory_text: Mrs. Hudson told me how sad it was that I was leaving after all these years, and she mentioned she once went through a divorce herself, trying to relate to my situation.

grounded_facts: Watson articulates his relief and anticipation about leaving behind the unpredictable and dangerous life with Holmes.
memories.memory_text: I admitted to myself that I was actually looking forward to leading a normal life again, with regular office hours and emergencies that were medical, not murderous.

grounded_facts: A gunshot from the living room abruptly halts Watson's departure process and triggers immediate alarm.
memories.memory_text: I was in the middle of leaving when I heard a revolver shot from the living room; I immediately felt alarmed, saw Mrs. Hudson react, and rushed out with my diploma still in hand.

grounded_facts: Holmes waves off Mrs. Hudson's complaint about gunshots in the apartment, showing disregard for her authority.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes dismiss Mrs. Hudson's complaints about the gunshots, brushing her off when she confronted him about the damage.

grounded_facts: Watson calms Mrs. Hudson by offering to clean the mess and return her belongings.
memories.memory_text: I calmed Mrs. Hudson down by telling her I would clean up the mess and handed her my diploma while asking her to unpack my things.

grounded_facts: Holmes verbally acknowledges his deep, albeit reserved, affection for Watson, marking a rare emotional disclosure.
memories.memory_text: I remember Holmes telling me, in his usual reserved way, that he was very fond of me, which meant a great deal coming from him.

grounded_facts: Holmes tells Watson he would do anything to keep him around, affirming their bond.
memories.memory_text: I recall Holmes saying he would do anything to keep me around, and it reassured me that my presence truly mattered to him.

grounded_facts: Watson returns to Holmes's residence, possibly considering leaving due to Holmes's drug use, prompting a dramatic performance to retain him.
memories.memory_text: I returned to Holmes's residence, uncertain whether I should stay or leave because of his drug use, and for a moment I worried he wouldn't even try to stop me from walking out.

grounded_facts: Holmes uses a revolver to smash three bottles he presents as narcotics, but they are later revealed to be substitutes from his chemistry set, part of a performance to convince Watson of his recovery.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes use his revolver to smash three bottles he claimed were narcotics, and though I didn't know it at the time, they were actually substitutes from his chemistry set—he did it all to convince me he was recovering and to keep me by his side.

grounded_facts: Holmes secretly retrieves the real narcotics bottles from the violin case, revealing that the destroyed ones were fakes, indicating his continued dependency.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes open the violin case and pull out the three original narcotics bottles stashed around the edges, realizing the ones he destroyed were just substitutes.

grounded_facts: Holmes rejects attending the final performance of the Imperial Russian Ballet despite receiving anonymous tickets and a plea for help.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes reject the invitation outright, even after we got the anonymous tickets and that plea for help—he said he suspected a plot, and then admitted he just detests ballet.

grounded_facts: Watson urges Holmes to accept the invitation to the ballet, emphasizing its importance and rarity, but Holmes resists.
memories.memory_text: I urged Holmes to go, emphasizing how rare and important the performance was, but he resisted every argument I made.

grounded_facts: The final performance of the Imperial Russian Ballet, specifically Swan Lake, for which tickets are highly sought after.
memories.memory_text: I remember telling Holmes that it wasn't just any ballet—we were talking about Swan Lake, the final performance of the Imperial Russian Ballet, with tickets that had been sold out for months.

grounded_facts: Watson reveals that twelve men have died due to their obsession with Petrova, providing background on her dangerous allure.
memories.memory_text: I mentioned that twelve men have died for love of Petrova, caught up in their obsession with her.

grounded_facts: Rogozhin abruptly asks Holmes about family medical history, creating tension and suspicion.
memories.memory_text: I was present when Rogozhin abruptly asked Holmes about his health, and I quickly responded that Holmes was in excellent shape, though I could sense the tension that followed his odd line of questioning.

grounded_facts: A live performance of Swan Lake at the theatre, attended by Holmes and Watson in evening dress.
memories.memory_text: I attended the Swan Lake performance with Holmes, both of us in evening dress, and I watched the stage through my opera glasses before handing them to him; I remarked on the man who fell from the gallery, and we stayed through the pas-de-deux to the ovation.

grounded_facts: Rogozhin formally extends an invitation for Holmes to meet Madame Petrova privately after the performance.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Rogozhin that Madame Petrova requested Holmes's presence after the performance, and he invited me to amuse myself with vodka, caviar, and the girls while Holmes went to her dressing room.

grounded_facts: A backstage gathering after the show, featuring food, drink, and socializing among cast and crew, where Holmes is summoned to meet Petrova.
memories.memory_text: After the show, I joined the backstage gathering with food and drink, where Rogozhin told me to amuse myself while Holmes met Petrova, so I made a playful remark about the ballerinas' po-pos and patted a couple with my cane.

grounded_facts: Watson humorously compliments the ballerinas' 'lovely po-pos' while patting them with his cane, after confirming they don't understand English.
memories.memory_text: I made a humorous remark about the ballerinas' lovely po-pos after checking they didn't understand English, then gave a couple of them a playful tap with my cane.

grounded_facts: Holmes accepts the invitation to meet Madame Petrova after the performance, indicating willingness to take on her case despite lack of initial details.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed Holmes accept the invitation and walk with Rogozhin toward Madame Petrova's dressing room, showing he was ready to take on her case even without knowing the details.

grounded_facts: Petrova visually assesses Holmes from head to toe after their initial greeting.
memories.memory_text: I noticed Petrova appraising Holmes from head to toe after they greeted each other, as if sizing him up.

grounded_facts: Petrova gifts Holmes a Stradivarius violin as a token of appreciation for services to be rendered.
memories.memory_text: I saw Petrova give Holmes a Stradivarius violin through Rogozhin, who said it was a gift from her for services to be rendered.

grounded_facts: Petrova reveals she is retiring from ballet to focus on motherhood.
memories.memory_text: I heard Rogozhin tell Holmes that Petrova was retiring from ballet to focus on motherhood.

grounded_facts: Watson briefly enters the dressing room, drunk and festive, asking about the meaning of 'prokanzik'.
memories.memory_text: I remember stumbling into the dressing room, feeling merry and a bit drunk, with a flower behind my ear, and asking Holmes what 'prokanzik' meant—Rogozhin answered it meant 'You little devil,' and I smiled, feeling oddly pleased before hurrying off.

grounded_facts: Holmes indirectly reveals his romantic relationship with Dr. Watson to decline Petrova's proposal.
Holmes refuses Petrova's proposal to father her child, citing his relationship with Watson and sexual orientation.
memories.memory_text: I later learned that Holmes told Petrova he wasn’t a free man and indirectly admitted we were in a romantic relationship to turn down her proposal, which surprised me—I didn’t know he would say such a thing.

grounded_facts: A private celebration following Petrova's final ballet performance, held in her dressing room and extending into a larger party.
memories.memory_text: I was at the private celebration in Petrova's dressing room after her final performance, which later turned into a wild party where I ended up dancing with several people.

grounded_facts: Holmes tries to get Watson to leave the party, but Watson refuses and continues dancing.
memories.memory_text: I was in the middle of dancing when Holmes came up and told me it was time to go home, but I refused and kept dancing with the girls.

grounded_facts: Rogozhin tells Watson that everyone now believes he is in a romantic relationship with Holmes, based on Holmes's earlier disclosure.
memories.memory_text: I asked Rogozhin what was happening, and he told me that everyone believed I was in a romantic relationship with Holmes because Holmes had told them about us.

grounded_facts: Watson is gradually abandoned by female dance partners, learns that a rumor about his romantic relationship with Holmes has spread, and reacts emotionally by drinking Rogozhin's vodka.
memories.memory_text: I kept dancing, but the girls started staring and whispering, then they all left me — I ended up only dancing with male partners, and when I realized something was wrong, I felt a chill and grabbed Rogozhin's vodka to steady myself.

grounded_facts: Watson repeatedly calls Holmes' name upon entering the flat, indicating urgency or need to locate him.
memories.memory_text: I called Holmes' name as soon as I came into the flat, needing to find him right away.

grounded_facts: Holmes steps out from a shadowy corner, admitting he used the machine to avoid Watson's anger, thus ending the pretense.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes step out from a shadowy corner, standing there as if nothing had happened, after I found the smoking machine.

grounded_facts: Watson realizes the figure in the chair is not Holmes but a mechanical device used for smoking, revealing Holmes' deception.
memories.memory_text: I realized the figure in the chair wasn't Holmes at all, but a smoking machine—he had tricked me, hiding while I thought he was ignoring me.

grounded_facts: In fury, Watson throws the smoking machine to the floor after learning of Holmes' deception.
memories.memory_text: In my fury, I threw the smoking machine to the floor when I realized Holmes had been deceiving me the whole time.

grounded_facts: Holmes apologizes but justifies his actions by claiming he was avoiding a madwoman.
memories.memory_text: Holmes told me he was sorry, but he claimed he faked his absence to avoid a madwoman, as if that could justify his actions.

grounded_facts: Watson angrily blames Holmes for spreading lies and humiliating him.
memories.memory_text: I blamed Holmes for the lies he spread, shouting at him about the damage done to me—my feelings, my standing in society, everything.

grounded_facts: Holmes downplays Watson's fears of scandal by suggesting St. Petersburg gossip is trivial.
memories.memory_text: I remember Holmes telling me not to worry about the gossip in St. Petersburg, as if it were nothing serious.

grounded_facts: Watson expresses fear that false rumors of a romantic relationship will destroy his reputation and pension.
memories.memory_text: I expressed my fear that these rumors would ruin my reputation and cost me my pension if they reached my old regiment.

grounded_facts: Watson confronts Holmes about a prank that led to damaging public rumors implying a romantic relationship between them.
memories.memory_text: I confronted Holmes about that wretched prank he pulled, which spread vile rumors about us—I demanded to know what he was thinking, how he could disgrace me like that and risk my reputation.

grounded_facts: Holmes draws attention to the flower behind Watson's ear, prompting Watson to discard it.
memories.memory_text: I recall Holmes pointing out the flower behind my ear, and I immediately took it out when he mentioned it.

grounded_facts: In a moment of panic, Watson suggests he and Holmes get married to quell gossip, later rejecting the idea.
memories.memory_text: In a moment of panic, I suggested to Holmes that we get married to stop the gossip, though I later dismissed the idea and tried to salvage my honor by mentioning women who could vouch for me.

grounded_facts: Holmes admits to Watson that there have been women in his life, then clarifies that Watson is being presumptuous.
memories.memory_text: Holmes told me there have been women in his life, but then said I was being presumptuous, which left me feeling rebuffed.

grounded_facts: Watson asks Holmes about his romantic history, seeking reassurance about their reputations.
memories.memory_text: I asked Holmes about his past relationships, hoping for reassurance, but he told me I was being presumptuous—leaving me embarrassed and deflated.

grounded_facts: Watson asks Holmes if he has ever had relationships with women.
memories.memory_text: I asked Holmes if he had ever had relationships with women, hoping I wasn't being presumptuous.

grounded_facts: Holmes asks Gabrielle why she came to 221B Baker Street, attempting to extract information about her intentions.
memories.memory_text: I was present when Holmes asked the young lady why she had come to our address, and she replied that she did not remember.

grounded_facts: A cabbie delivers a mysterious wet and injured woman named Gabrielle to 221B Baker Street, claiming she was pulled from the river and had the address in her hand.
memories.memory_text: The cabbie told me he pulled the woman, Gabrielle, from the river near Westminster Bridge and brought her to 221B because he found the address in her hand.

grounded_facts: The cabbie insists on being paid two-and-six for transporting Gabrielle, threatening to abandon her otherwise.
memories.memory_text: I heard the cabbie demand two-and-six from us, threatening to throw her back in the river if we didn't pay.

grounded_facts: Watson pays the cabbie two-and-six for bringing Gabrielle to 221B, accepting responsibility for her.
memories.memory_text: I paid the cabbie two-and-six from my own pocket to secure Gabrielle's safety and take responsibility for her.

grounded_facts: Gabrielle is identified as a woman in her early thirties with a bruise on her temple, wet hair, wrapped in a blanket, wearing a wedding ring, and unable to recall who she is or why she was at the river.
memories.memory_text: I saw that Gabrielle was a woman in her early thirties, with wet hair, a bruise on her temple, wrapped in a blanket, wearing a wedding ring, and unable to say anything but 'I don't know' when asked who she was.

grounded_facts: A sudden late-night visit by a cabbie delivering an unconscious woman to 221B Baker Street, disrupting the quiet evening of Holmes and Watson.
memories.memory_text: I was with Holmes when the bell rang late at night, and I answered the door to find a cabbie bringing in an unconscious woman, which disrupted our quiet evening.

grounded_facts: After payment, Gabrielle is led by Watson up the stairs into the upper rooms of 221B Baker Street to get out of her wet clothes.
Watson physically supports Gabrielle by putting his arm around her and offering to help her change out of wet clothes.
memories.memory_text: I noticed Gabrielle was shivering, so I put my arm around her and told her I’d help her out of those wet clothes, then led her up the stairs to get warm.

grounded_facts: Gabrielle is brought to Holmes and Watson's living room, suffering from a head injury, exposure, and shock after being found in or near the Thames.
memories.memory_text: I led Gabrielle to a chair by the fireplace and settled her in, seeing she was suffering from shock and exposure; I noticed the nasty blow on her head and realized she had been found in or near the Thames.

grounded_facts: Watson diagnoses Gabrielle with a concussion leading to temporary amnesia based on her head wound and mental state.
memories.memory_text: I diagnosed Gabrielle with a concussion based on her head wound, and I concluded it was likely causing temporary amnesia, so I began cleaning and treating her injury with antiseptic.

grounded_facts: Holmes deduces Gabrielle's nationality and origin by examining a label inside her dress collar that reads 'BAZAAR MODERN, Bruxelles'.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes turn back the collar of Gabrielle's dress and noticed the label inside that read 'BAZAAR MODERN, Bruxelles', which made me realize she was from Belgium.

grounded_facts: Holmes removes Gabrielle's wedding ring and reads the engraving 'Gabrielle - Emile', identifying her name and her husband's name.
memories.memory_text: I watched Holmes slip the wedding ring off Gabrielle's finger and examine it with a magnifying glass, where he found the engraving 'Gabrielle - Emile', learning her name and her husband's name.

grounded_facts: Holmes aggressively questions Gabrielle about her name, husband, and events at the river, causing her to burst into sobs.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes press Gabrielle with rapid questions about her name, her husband, and what happened at the river, and I watched her burst into sobs under the strain.

grounded_facts: Watson intervenes to stop Holmes' harsh questioning, asserting that Gabrielle must not be distressed further.
memories.memory_text: I stepped in and told Holmes that he had gone too far, saying, 'That's enough, Holmes. I will not permit you to question her in this condition,' because I couldn't let her suffer more.

grounded_facts: Watson prepares a sleeping potion and administers it to Gabrielle, who is then taken to bed by Mrs. Hudson.
memories.memory_text: I prepared a sleeping potion for Gabrielle by mixing a spoonful of white powder from my medical bag into her tea, and then I told Mrs. Hudson to put her to bed in my room.

grounded_facts: A medical and investigative session in which Gabrielle is examined, diagnosed, and partially identified by Holmes and Watson.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed the full medical and investigative session where I introduced myself as Dr. Watson, examined Gabrielle, and worked alongside Holmes as we gathered clues about her identity while I made sure she was cared for.

grounded_facts: Holmes suggests sending Gabrielle to a hospital, while Watson insists on keeping her for protection and treatment.
memories.memory_text: I insisted to Holmes that under no circumstances should Gabrielle be sent to a hospital because I can provide her medical care and, more importantly, she must be protected since there's already been an attempt on her life.

grounded_facts: Mrs. Hudson wakes Watson by clapping her hands and urging him to get up for breakfast.
Mrs. Hudson prepares breakfast and attempts to wake Watson.
memories.memory_text: I remember Mrs. Hudson waking me up by calling my name and telling me my porridge was getting lumpy, while she had already set the table and opened the curtains for breakfast.

grounded_facts: Watson is awakened by Mrs. Hudson and struggles to get up due to back pain.
memories.memory_text: I tried to get up when she called me, but my back seized up and I fell back onto the couch, moaning from the pain.

grounded_facts: Watson pleads with Mrs. Hudson to help relieve his back pain by applying pressure to his spine.
memories.memory_text: I pleaded with Mrs. Hudson to help me by pressing on my back, and I guided her to put her arms under mine and fold them behind my neck so she could adjust my spine.

grounded_facts: Mrs. Hudson applies pressure to Watson's back at his direction, resulting in a spinal adjustment with an audible snap.
memories.memory_text: I felt Mrs. Hudson press down on my back with her knee, and then there was a distinct snap as the adjustment took place, which finally relieved my pain.

grounded_facts: Mrs. Hudson informs Watson that Gabrielle is no longer in her room.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Mrs. Hudson that Gabrielle was gone, and I could see the urgency in her voice.

grounded_facts: Watson discovers that Gabrielle is no longer in her bedroom, despite her clothes remaining.
memories.memory_text: I jumped up and saw the bed was empty myself, though her clothes were still there, which alarmed me.

grounded_facts: Mrs. Hudson checks on Gabrielle in her bedroom and discovers she is missing.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Mrs. Hudson that Gabrielle was gone, and I immediately got up to check her room, seeing that the bed was empty and her clothes were left behind.

grounded_facts: Watson shouts to alert Holmes that Gabrielle has disappeared.
memories.memory_text: I shouted to Holmes that Gabrielle was gone, calling out as loud as I could to alert him.

grounded_facts: Watson prepares to enter Holmes' bedroom to alert him but freezes upon seeing something inside.
memories.memory_text: I was about to step into Holmes' room to tell him, but I froze when I saw something inside that stopped me in my tracks.

grounded_facts: Holmes enters the living room carrying Gabrielle Valladon's suitcase, which he has retrieved using a luggage ticket clue from her hand.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes come into the living room carrying Gabrielle Valladon's suitcase, which he must have retrieved using the luggage ticket clue, and he set it down on the couch as Mrs. Hudson and I approached.

grounded_facts: Holmes sarcastically tells Mrs. Hudson to wipe her disapproving expression, prompting her to leave angrily.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes tell Mrs. Hudson to go to the kitchen and wipe that look of disapproval off her face, and she stormed out, clearly upset.

grounded_facts: Holmes uses a butter-knife to force open the locks of the suitcase and begins examining its contents.
memories.memory_text: I watched Holmes use a butter-knife I handed him to force open the suitcase locks, and then we both began examining the contents, starting with a pink feathered negligee and sorting through the rest of the clothes.

grounded_facts: Holmes begins active investigation of Gabrielle Valladon's case by retrieving and examining her suitcase.
memories.memory_text: I realized Holmes had begun actively investigating Gabrielle Valladon's case when he brought the suitcase back and started going through it right in front of me.

grounded_facts: Gabrielle emerges from Holmes's bedroom, confirms her identity as Gabrielle Valladon, and identifies the man in the photo as her husband, Emile Valladon.
memories.memory_text: I saw Gabrielle emerge from Holmes's bedroom, still dazed, and I heard Holmes confirm her identity before asking if the man in the photo was her husband Emile Valladon, to which she simply said yes.

grounded_facts: Holmes tells Gabrielle that Watson is the handsome one, causing Watson to smile and twirl his mustache.
memories.memory_text: I smiled and twirled my mustache when Holmes told Gabrielle that I was the handsome one.

grounded_facts: Gabrielle Valladon is formally interviewed by Holmes and Watson, during which she provides her backstory and reveals an attack.
memories.memory_text: I was present when Gabrielle Valladon was formally interviewed by Holmes, and I heard her tell us about her marriage in the Congo and her husband the mining engineer, confirming she came to us for help.

grounded_facts: Holmes correctly deduces Gabrielle's wedding location by noting her copper ring.
memories.memory_text: I watched Holmes pick up Gabrielle's wedding ring from the chemistry table and note that it was made of copper, from which he deduced where she had been married.

grounded_facts: Gabrielle reveals she was attacked with chloroform and thrown into the water while en route to consult Holmes.
memories.memory_text: I heard Gabrielle describe how she was attacked with chloroform and thrown into the water while on her way to see Holmes.

grounded_facts: Holmes has Gabrielle address a letter with an empty sheet inside to be sent to Ashdown Street.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes have Gabrielle address a letter with an empty sheet inside and asked him if we were really sending an empty sheet to an empty shop.

grounded_facts: Holmes asks Watson for hammer and chisel to break into the skylight.
memories.memory_text: Holmes told me to hand him the hammer and chisel so he could break into the skylight.

grounded_facts: Holmes breaks into the shop by sawing through the iron bars of a skylight, chips away cement, and swings the grill open to enter.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes saw through the iron bars of the skylight, chip away the cement, and swing the grill open before dropping inside.

grounded_facts: Holmes catches and supports Gabrielle as she is lowered through the skylight, briefly holding her.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes catch Gabrielle as she was lowered through the skylight and briefly hold her around the waist before setting her down.

grounded_facts: Holmes, Watson, and Gabrielle illegally enter the empty shop through the skylight to investigate its purpose.
memories.memory_text: I was part of the team that entered the empty shop illegally through the rear skylight to investigate what was going on inside.

grounded_facts: Watson helps Gabrielle through the skylight, and Holmes assists her descent; Watson follows shortly after.
memories.memory_text: I helped Gabrielle through the skylight and watched Holmes assist her descent, then I followed them down into the shop.

grounded_facts: Watson uncovers a tarpaulin to reveal a large cage containing about a hundred canaries.
memories.memory_text: I uncovered a tarpaulin and found a large cage filled with about a hundred canaries, which made me wonder if this place had once been a pet shop.

grounded_facts: A postman delivers a letter through the door slot, landing on a dusty floor with unusual tracks.
memories.memory_text: I saw a postman deliver a letter through the door slot, and it landed on a dusty floor with strange double tracks that curved to the door and back.

grounded_facts: Holmes reassembles his tools into a cane, indicating concealment and preparedness.
memories.memory_text: I watched Holmes reassemble his tools into a cane, which showed he was preparing to conceal them.

grounded_facts: Gabrielle expresses concern about payment, revealing her purse is lost in the Thames.
Gabrielle tells Holmes she cannot pay because her purse is lost in the Thames.
memories.memory_text: I heard Gabrielle tell Holmes she couldn't pay because her purse was lost in the Thames.

grounded_facts: Holmes leads Watson and Gabrielle to conceal themselves beside the rear door as the old woman enters.
memories.memory_text: I followed Holmes as he led Gabrielle and me to hide beside the rear door when the old woman arrived.

grounded_facts: An old woman in a wheelchair enters, uncovers the cage, and feeds the canaries.
memories.memory_text: I saw the old woman in the wheelchair enter the mews, uncover the canary cage with a pulley, and feed the birds from a paper bag and pitcher.

grounded_facts: Carters greet the woman and purchase two dozen canaries.
Two carters arrive and purchase two dozen canaries from the old woman.
memories.memory_text: I watched two carters arrive, greet the woman as 'Duchess,' and buy two dozen canaries, which they began transferring into a small cage lined with newspaper.

grounded_facts: Carters arrive to collect canaries for transport, part of a larger operation linked to Inverness.
memories.memory_text: I observed two carters arrive with a wagon, take canaries from the large cage into a small one lined with newspaper, and then drive away.

grounded_facts: An old woman in a wheelchair enters the shop to feed the canaries and maintain the cage.
memories.memory_text: I watched an old woman in a wheelchair come in, feed the canaries, and then leave after covering the cage and depositing a letter on it.

grounded_facts: Holmes and team notice the newspaper lining the small bird cage is the Inverness Courier, suggesting a location.
memories.memory_text: Holmes told me he noticed the newspaper at the bottom of the cage was the Inverness Courier, suggesting where the birds came from.

grounded_facts: Gabrielle discovers and hands Holmes a letter delivered to the shop that is addressed to him.
memories.memory_text: I saw Gabrielle notice the letter left on the cage and realized it was addressed to Holmes when she handed it to him.

grounded_facts: A letter is delivered to the shop and later retrieved, part of a covert communication system.
memories.memory_text: I saw a letter delivered through the door slot, and later noticed it was left on top of the covered cage before the old woman wheeled away.

grounded_facts: Holmes opens and reads a letter from Mycroft summoning him to the Diogenes Club at 11 a.m.
memories.memory_text: I watched Holmes open the letter from Mycroft and read the message summoning us to the Diogenes Club at 11 a.m.

grounded_facts: Holmes tells Watson to reset his watch after reading Mycroft's letter.
memories.memory_text: Holmes told me to reset my watch after reading Mycroft's letter, suggesting mine was wrong despite showing 10:43.

grounded_facts: Watson tells Holmes he is apprehensive about confronting Madame Valladon.
memories.memory_text: I told Holmes that I was apprehensive about confronting Madame Valladon.

grounded_facts: Holmes tells Watson that Madame Valladon is safe with Mrs. Hudson.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Holmes that Madame Valladon is safe with Mrs. Hudson.

grounded_facts: Holmes and Watson visit the Diogenes Club to meet Mycroft.
Holmes and Watson arrive at the Diogenes Club and begin entering the building.
memories.memory_text: I arrived with Holmes at the Diogenes Club and we began entering the building to meet Mycroft.

grounded_facts: The porter attempts to have Holmes and Watson sign in, but they ignore him and proceed directly upstairs.
memories.memory_text: I ignored the porter's request to sign in and followed Holmes directly up the staircase.

grounded_facts: Holmes and Watson enter the Diogenes Club to meet Mycroft Holmes in the upstairs study.
memories.memory_text: I entered the Diogenes Club with Holmes to meet Mycroft in his upstairs study.

grounded_facts: A private meeting between Mycroft Holmes, Sherlock Holmes, and Dr. Watson in the study of the Diogenes Club.
memories.memory_text: I was present in the study of the Diogenes Club for a private meeting between Mycroft and Sherlock Holmes.

grounded_facts: Mycroft informs Holmes that the engineer case involves national security and is being handled by his organization, implying government authority.
Mycroft explicitly tells Holmes to cease investigating the engineer case due to national security concerns.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Mycroft that the engineer case involved national security and that his organization was handling it, and he explicitly instructed Holmes to stop investigating it.

grounded_facts: Mycroft receives and responds to a telegram with cryptic instructions, indicating covert operations.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mycroft receive a telegram and dictate a response with cryptic instructions about boxes going to Glennahurich and a red runner to the castle, which made me suspect he was handling some covert operation.

grounded_facts: Mycroft explicitly states that his warning is not a suggestion but an order from Her Majesty's government.
memories.memory_text: I was present when Mycroft told Sherlock that his warning wasn't just a suggestion, but an order backed by the authority of Her Majesty's government.

grounded_facts: After the confrontation, Mycroft ends the meeting with formal courtesy.
memories.memory_text: I was present when Mycroft ended the meeting with formal courtesy, excusing himself from the conversation.

grounded_facts: Mycroft hands back Holmes' cane, calling it a 'tool-kit' in a teasing manner.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mycroft tease Holmes by calling his cane a 'tool-kit' before tossing it back to him.

grounded_facts: Instead of answering Watson's question, Holmes shifts focus by explaining the etymology of 'Glennahurich'.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes shift the conversation when I asked about dropping the case, instead asking me what 'Glennahurich' suggested to me.

grounded_facts: Holmes deciphers the meaning of the name 'Glennahurich' as 'Valley of the Yew Tree', suggesting a geographical destination.
memories.memory_text: Holmes told me that 'Glennahurich' meant 'Valley of the Yew Tree', breaking it down from Scottish words—glen for valley, na for 'of the', and hurich for yew tree.

grounded_facts: Holmes concludes that the three boxes are destined for the Valley of the Yew Tree, based on his interpretation of 'Glennahurich'.
memories.memory_text: Holmes told me that the three boxes were destined for the Valley of the Yew Tree, based on his interpretation of the name.

grounded_facts: Watson repeatedly asks Holmes whether he is truly dropping the case, showing concern and seeking reassurance.
memories.memory_text: I asked Holmes again if he was dropping the case, because I needed to know whether we were really stepping away from it.

grounded_facts: Upon attempting to enter 221B, Holmes and Watson are met with a revolver pointed at them through the door, held by Mrs. Hudson.
memories.memory_text: I was with Holmes when we returned to 221B, and as I turned the key and started to open the door, a chain stopped it from opening fully—then a revolver appeared through the gap, pointed right at us.

grounded_facts: Holmes speaks calmly to Mrs. Hudson to prevent her from shooting, using humor to defuse the situation.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mrs. Hudson behind the door with the gun, and I was startled, but Holmes spoke calmly and joked, saying not to shoot because she’d lose two good tenants, which eased the tension.

grounded_facts: Holmes relieves Mrs. Hudson of the gun she was holding, indicating a transfer of responsibility or security.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes take the gun from Mrs. Hudson as we stepped into the vestibule.

grounded_facts: Mrs. Hudson expresses frustration about the absurd difficulty of doing embroidery while holding a gun.
memories.memory_text: I heard Mrs. Hudson complain to me about how hard it was to do embroidery while holding a gun.

grounded_facts: Holmes informs Mrs. Hudson that the gun she was holding was not loaded, altering her understanding of the risk she faced.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Holmes that the gun Mrs. Hudson had been holding wasn't loaded.

grounded_facts: Watson presses Holmes on whether he intends to disobey Mycroft's orders, emphasizing the political stakes.
memories.memory_text: I pressed Holmes on whether he intended to disobey Mycroft's orders, reminding him that it wouldn't just be family he was defying, but Her Majesty's government itself.

grounded_facts: Gabrielle is waiting at the flat's doorway and immediately asks for updates, signaling urgency and her dependence on their investigation.
Gabrielle immediately questions the returning pair for any updates on the investigation.
memories.memory_text: I saw Gabrielle waiting in the doorway of our flat as Holmes and I returned, and she immediately asked us if we had any news or found anything out, making it clear how urgently she needed updates from us.

grounded_facts: Holmes corrects Gabrielle's misunderstanding by revealing the staged nature of her departure.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Holmes corrects Gabrielle's misunderstanding by revealing the staged nature of her departure.

grounded_facts: Holmes informs Gabrielle and Watson that they will stage her departure on the boat-train to Brussels while secretly rerouting to Inverness under assumed identities.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Holmes informs Gabrielle and Watson that they will stage her departure on the boat-train to Brussels while secretly rerouting to Inverness under assumed identities.

grounded_facts: After misunderstanding Holmes's intention, Gabrielle realizes the ruse, thanks him, and apologizes for doubting him.
Gabrielle expresses regret for doubting Holmes and thanks him with a kiss on the cheek.
memories.memory_text: I saw Gabrielle realize Holmes had only pretended to send her away, and she turned to him, thanking him and apologizing for doubting him before kissing him on the cheek.

grounded_facts: Watson locates Gabrielle's missing glove after she searches for it.
memories.memory_text: I found Gabrielle's missing glove by looking under the couch and handed it to her.

grounded_facts: Gabrielle begins packing and retrieves her belongings, including her missing glove.
memories.memory_text: I saw Gabrielle begin packing and searching for her belongings, and I helped her by finding the glove she was looking for.

grounded_facts: A shared trip by train involving Watson and his employers, as well as other passengers including monks, traveling toward Inverness.
memories.memory_text: I remember that I'm traveling by train with my employers toward Inverness, and we're sharing the journey with several monks who seem to be heading the same way.

grounded_facts: Watson initiates friendly conversation with the monk, apologizing for stepping on his foot and attempting small talk.
memories.memory_text: I apologized for stepping on the monk's foot and tried to make small talk, asking if they were going to Scotland too, then mentioning that my master and mistress and I are on our way to Inverness—I even commented on the beautiful country to keep the conversation going.

grounded_facts: Watson infers from the monk's gesture and lack of response that he is observing a vow of silence, likely identifying him as a Trappist.
memories.memory_text: I saw the monk look up from his Bible, point to his lips, and shake his head when I spoke, so I realized he must be observing a vow of silence—likely a Trappist.

grounded_facts: Watson observes the open page in the monk's Bible and comments on the coincidence with a recent conversation about 'Johan'.
memories.memory_text: I glanced over and saw the monk reading the Book of Jonah, and I thought it was a funny coincidence since we'd just been talking about Johan that morning.

grounded_facts: Watson points out the monk's reading of the Book of Jonah and references a morning conversation about 'Johan', then abandons the exchange.
memories.memory_text: I pointed out that he was reading Jonah and mentioned our earlier chat about Johan, but then I realized he wasn't going to respond, so I gave up and said, 'Never mind.'

grounded_facts: After failing to establish conversation, Watson becomes bored and decides to rest.
memories.memory_text: I tried to make conversation but realized it was futile, so I became bored and decided to rest, pulling down the shade and closing my eyes to try to sleep.

grounded_facts: A monk checks that Watson is asleep before leaving his seat.
memories.memory_text: I was asleep, and the monk beside me checked that I was out before getting up and moving away.

grounded_facts: Holmes, Gabrielle, and Watson arrive at Inverness station as the Highland Express departs.
memories.memory_text: I arrived at Inverness station with Holmes and Gabrielle just as the Highland Express was pulling out, the last car vanishing into the steam.

grounded_facts: Holmes asks the baggageman for directions and distance to Glennahurich.
memories.memory_text: I was standing with Holmes and Gabrielle on the platform at Inverness when I heard him ask the baggageman how to get to Glennahurich and how far it was.

grounded_facts: Watson suggests Glennahurich could be a nice picnic spot, misunderstanding its true nature.
memories.memory_text: I suggested that Glennahurich might be a nice spot for a picnic if it had a view, thinking it could be a scenic place.

grounded_facts: The group learns that Glennahurich, a destination they are inquiring about, is a cemetery and not suitable for a picnic.
memories.memory_text: I learned from the baggageman that Glennahurich is a cemetery, not a picnic spot, when he told us it was about a mile out of town and then said, 'Because it's a cemetery.'

grounded_facts: Holmes, Gabrielle, and Watson observe a funeral with three coffins and note the absence of mourners and flowers.
A funeral for three unidentified individuals — one adult and two children-sized — takes place with no mourners present.
memories.memory_text: I was with Holmes and Gabrielle when we saw a funeral with three coffins—one large and two smaller ones—being taken to graves with no mourners or flowers, and I pointed out the three boxes to Holmes, feeling it might be a key clue we were following.

grounded_facts: Holmes questions the grave-digger about the deceased and the circumstances of their death.
memories.memory_text: I was present when Holmes questioned the grave-digger about the deceased and how they had died.

grounded_facts: Holmes questions a grave-digger who reveals the deceased were a father and two sons found floating in the loch, though locals suspect the Loch Ness Monster.
memories.memory_text: I was told by the grave-digger that the deceased were a father and two sons found floating in the loch, and though he mentioned locals suspect the Loch Ness Monster, he seemed to believe they died of fright.

grounded_facts: Four adult midgets, appearing as boys, silently lay flowers on the two small graves and pray.
memories.memory_text: I saw four small figures approaching the graves, laying flowers on the two smaller ones and praying, and though I first thought they were boys, I was startled when they turned and I realized they had the faces of grown men despite their size.

grounded_facts: Holmes deduces that the four flower-laying 'boys' are actually adult midgets, likely the missing acrobat brothers, and infers the third grave's occupant is unknown.
memories.memory_text: I saw the four figures laying flowers on the graves and first thought they were boys, but then noticed their mature faces when they turned, and I realized with Holmes's help that they were actually adult midgets, likely the missing acrobats, though I still wasn't sure who the third grave belonged to.

grounded_facts: Holmes deduces the midgets are the brothers of the deceased and part of a missing circus act.
memories.memory_text: Holmes told me the midgets were brothers of the deceased and part of a missing circus act, and when he asked if I remembered the six missing acrobat brothers, I recalled that case we had turned down.

grounded_facts: Holmes raises the unresolved question of who is buried in the third grave, implying the two small graves may not have contained the father's sons.
memories.memory_text: I was with Holmes at the gravesite when he turned to me and asked, 'The question now is -- who's in the third grave?' It struck me then that the small coffins might not have held the father's sons after all.

grounded_facts: Holmes leads an exhumation at night in Glennahurich Cemetery to inspect the coffin of Emile Valladon.
memories.memory_text: I was with Holmes at Glennahurich Cemetery that night, kneeling beside the grave while he worked below, and I held the bullseye lantern ready for whatever he might need.

grounded_facts: Gabrielle screams and collapses upon recognizing her husband's body, and is caught by Watson.
memories.memory_text: I was holding the lantern and kneeling beside the grave when Gabrielle screamed and collapsed; I caught her before she hit the ground.

grounded_facts: Watson informs Holmes that Gabrielle has fainted.
memories.memory_text: I told Holmes, 'She's fainted,' right after I caught Gabrielle.

grounded_facts: Holmes confirms the corpse is Emile Valladon based on facial recognition.
memories.memory_text: I heard Holmes say he recognized the body as Emile Valladon, though I didn't confirm it myself.

grounded_facts: Holmes asks Watson to hand him the lantern.
memories.memory_text: I handed Holmes the lantern when he asked me for it.

grounded_facts: Holmes pries open the coffin lid, revealing the corpse of Emile Valladon.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes pry open the coffin lid and reveal the corpse inside, and I passed down my lantern so he could shine the beam along the body to examine it closely.

grounded_facts: Holmes notices the green discoloration of Valladon's wedding ring and the presence of three bleached white canaries at his feet.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes notice the green discoloration on Valladon's wedding ring and the three bleached white canaries at his feet inside the coffin.

grounded_facts: Holmes, Watson, and Gabrielle arrive at the Caledonian Hotel by carriage at dawn.
memories.memory_text: I arrived at the Caledonian Hotel by carriage at dawn, sitting beside the coachman while Holmes and Gabrielle rode in the passenger seat with our luggage strapped to the back, and then I got out with them.

grounded_facts: The manager points out the view of the loch and comments on the morning mist.
memories.memory_text: The manager told me and the others that we had a lovely view of the loch, though I could barely see it through the morning mist he mentioned.

grounded_facts: The manager opens the curtains to reveal the view of the lake and provides a guidebook for sightseeing.
memories.memory_text: I saw the manager open the curtains to reveal the lake view, and then he offered us a guidebook for sightseeing, saying it would help us find local points of interest.

grounded_facts: The manager gestures and speaks to Watson, indicating he should follow to his room.
memories.memory_text: The manager nodded to me and said, 'This way, please. I will show you to your room,' so I knew I was to follow him.

grounded_facts: The characters arrive at the hotel and are being settled into their rooms at dawn, with the manager assisting in orientation.
memories.memory_text: I was bringing our bags into the room when the manager nodded to me and said, 'This way, please. I will show you to your room,' so I followed him to get settled.

grounded_facts: Watson follows the manager out of the room to be shown to his own room.
memories.memory_text: I picked up my suitcase and followed the manager out of the room to be shown to my own room.

grounded_facts: Watson learns his room is in the attic, not the basement, and the privy is in the basement.
Manager corrects Watson's belief about his room location and adds a detail about the privy.
memories.memory_text: I assumed the manager was putting me in the basement, but he told me my room is actually in the attic and that it's the privy that's in the basement.

grounded_facts: Watson urgently moves from the attic to Holmes' room and opens the door forcefully.
memories.memory_text: I came dashing down the narrow stairs from the attic, racing toward Holmes' room because I urgently needed to reach Mr. Ashdown.

grounded_facts: Watson urgently tells Holmes that he saw the monster in the lake from the attic.
Watson claims to have seen the monster from the attic and reports it to Holmes.
memories.memory_text: I saw the monster in the lake from the attic and I urgently told Holmes about it.

grounded_facts: Watson asks Holmes about the location of the telescope.
memories.memory_text: I asked Holmes where the telescope was because I needed it to get a better look.

grounded_facts: Watson takes a small telescope from Holmes' suitcase.
Watson rushes through the French window to the balcony to look at the lake.
memories.memory_text: I took the small telescope from Holmes' suitcase and rushed through the French window to the balcony to look at the lake.

grounded_facts: Watson uses a telescope to observe a mysterious, monster-like figure with a long neck moving in the lake through the mist.
memories.memory_text: I used the telescope to look across the lake and saw a shadowy figure with a long, monster-like neck moving through the mist.

grounded_facts: Watson becomes excited and claims to see the monster in the lake through the telescope.
memories.memory_text: I got so excited when I saw what I believed was the monster in the lake through the telescope that I almost dropped it, and I called out to Holmes, 'There it is! There it is!'

grounded_facts: Watson hands the telescope to Holmes and urges him to see the monster for himself.
memories.memory_text: I handed the telescope to Holmes and told him to look for himself, hoping he'd see the monster too.

grounded_facts: Holmes uses the telescope to look at the lake for signs of the monster, but sees nothing.
memories.memory_text: I watched Holmes look through the telescope at the lake, but he saw nothing, which made me anxious.

grounded_facts: Watson takes the telescope from Holmes to look at the lake himself.
memories.memory_text: I took the telescope from Holmes so I could look myself and verify what was on the lake.

grounded_facts: Watson disputes Holmes' claim of seeing nothing by taking the telescope to verify for himself.
memories.memory_text: I questioned Holmes when he said he saw nothing, so I took the telescope from him and looked toward the lake myself to check.

grounded_facts: Holmes and Watson use a telescope from the balcony to observe the lake, searching for a previously sighted object.
memories.memory_text: Holmes and I used the telescope from the balcony to search the lake for the object I had seen earlier.

grounded_facts: Watson reports that the object he previously saw on the lake is no longer visible.
memories.memory_text: I looked through the telescope and reported to Holmes that the object I had seen was gone.

grounded_facts: Holmes expresses skepticism about the prior existence of the object Watson claims to have seen.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Holmes that the object I saw might never have existed, when he said, 'Gone? Maybe it was never there.'

grounded_facts: Holmes implies Watson may have imagined the object, invoking the rationalist spirit of the century.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Holmes that we are living in the Nineteenth Century, implying I may have imagined the object I saw.

grounded_facts: Holmes steps back into the room, ending his engagement with the outdoor observation.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes step back into the room, ending his observation outside.

grounded_facts: Holmes deduces that Monsieur Valladon did not drown but died of asphyxiation due to chlorine gas exposure, based on evidence from the wedding rings and canary discoloration.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Holmes that Monsieur Valladon did not drown, but died of asphyxiation from chlorine gas, which he deduced from the green discoloration on the wedding ring and the bleached canaries.

grounded_facts: Watson counters Holmes's dismissal of his sighting by pointing out the contradiction in Holmes criticizing him for lacking imagination while now calling his observation a figment.
memories.memory_text: I confronted Holmes, telling him he's the least logical man I know because he can't claim my observation is a figment of my imagination when he's always said I have no imagination at all.

grounded_facts: Holmes, Gabrielle, and Watson leave the hotel on bicycles, beginning a journey to investigate castles.
memories.memory_text: I remember leaving the hotel on my bicycle with Holmes and Gabrielle, riding past a stone wall, through a copse of trees, and along a steep road where we had to navigate through a flock of sheep before continuing on a causeway away from a castle.

grounded_facts: A midday outdoor meal by the lake involving Holmes, Gabrielle, and Watson.
Holmes, Gabrielle, and Watson are having a picnic by the lake, with food spread out and wine being poured.
memories.memory_text: I was at a picnic by the lake with Holmes and Gabrielle, where we had food spread out and I was pouring wine.

grounded_facts: Holmes politely asks Watson to pass the cranberry sauce during the picnic.
memories.memory_text: Holmes asked me politely to pass the cranberry sauce during our meal.

grounded_facts: Seven Trappist monks appear on the road above, walking in single file toward a bridge over the narrowing lake.
memories.memory_text: I saw seven Trappist monks walking in single file on the road above, making their way toward the bridge over the narrowing lake.

grounded_facts: Watson calls out and waves to the monks, recognizing them from a previous train ride, but they do not respond.
memories.memory_text: I called out and waved to the monks, remembering that I had spoken with them before on a train ride, but they didn't respond, which I knew was because they're Trappists and not allowed to talk.

grounded_facts: Gabrielle challenges Watson's dismissal of the castle by pointing out the presence of security measures, prompting further consideration.
memories.memory_text: I said the castle was just rubble and not worth bothering with, but Gabrielle challenged me by asking why they'd have precautions if it were truly insignificant.

grounded_facts: A brief observational visit by Holmes, Gabrielle, and Watson to Urquhart Castle during daylight, intended to assess access but aborted due to security measures.
Holmes, Gabrielle, and Watson arrive by bicycle at the gates of Urquhart Castle and observe warning signs and a guard, leading to their decision to leave the main entrance.
memories.memory_text: I arrived by bicycle with Holmes and Gabrielle at Urquhart Castle during daylight, and we quickly decided to leave the main entrance after seeing a guard, warning signs, and security measures.

grounded_facts: Holmes decides to bypass the main entrance after being deterred by the guard and warning sign, opting instead to find an alternative way in.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes react to the guard and warning sign by deciding to bypass the main entrance, and he signaled for us to leave right away.

grounded_facts: Holmes explains to Watson that since they cannot enter through the front, they will attempt entry via a tradesman's entrance.
memories.memory_text: Holmes told me that since we couldn't go in through the front, we would try entering via the tradesman's entrance instead.

grounded_facts: Holmes engages the guide in a discussion about the historical origins of Urquhart Castle to test his knowledge.
memories.memory_text: I was there when Holmes began questioning the guide about when Urquhart Castle was built, asking if it was under James the Second or Third, just to test his knowledge.

grounded_facts: Holmes realizes the guide incorrectly dated Urquhart Castle's construction, identifying it as 1500 under James the Fourth instead of the guide's claim of 1400 under James the Third.
memories.memory_text: Holmes told me the guide was wrong by a hundred years and one king—he said the castle was actually built in 1500 under James the Fourth, not earlier as the guide claimed.

grounded_facts: Holmes, Watson, and Gabrielle observe workmen transporting a birdcage and crates labeled 'SULPHURIC ACID - CORROSIVE' into the castle tower.
memories.memory_text: I saw the workmen carry a birdcage and crates labeled 'SULPHURIC ACID - CORROSIVE' into the castle tower while Gabrielle and I were with Holmes.

grounded_facts: Holmes deduces that the combination of sulphuric acid and saltwater could be used to generate chlorine gas, indicating a dangerous or malicious operation.
memories.memory_text: Holmes told me that sulphuric acid, when exposed to saltwater, produces chlorine gas, which made me realize the danger we were facing.

grounded_facts: Holmes asks Watson to clasp his hands to serve as a step for climbing scaffolding.
memories.memory_text: I clasped my hands as Holmes asked, so he could use them as a foothold to climb the scaffolding.

grounded_facts: Watson signals discomfort and fear upon seeing the guard's aggressive mastiffs.
memories.memory_text: I felt my heart race and cast anxious glances behind me as I hurried after Holmes and Gabrielle, the barking mastiffs making me fear we were in real danger.

grounded_facts: After observing suspicious activity and being noticed by guard dogs, Holmes leads Watson and Gabrielle in a swift departure from Urquhart Castle.
memories.memory_text: I saw suspicious activity at the castle, including men unloading a birdcage and crates marked with 'SULPHURIC ACID - CORROSIVE,' and when the guard dogs noticed us, Holmes led Gabrielle and me in a swift retreat.

grounded_facts: Holmes, Watson, and Gabrielle arrive at Urquhart Castle intending to tour the site, but instead observe suspicious restoration activities.
memories.memory_text: I came with Holmes and Gabrielle to tour Urquhart Castle, but instead I saw workers unloading a birdcage and crates marked with 'SULPHURIC ACID - CORROSIVE,' which made me uneasy.

grounded_facts: When Watson jumps up upon seeing the monster, Holmes grabs his arm and pulls him back to prevent panic and maintain control.
memories.memory_text: When I jumped up in shock after seeing the monster, Holmes grabbed my arm and pulled me back into my seat, keeping me from doing something reckless.

grounded_facts: Holmes asks Watson for his stethoscope to listen for underwater activity after the monster submerges.
memories.memory_text: I remember Holmes asking me for my stethoscope, and I handed it to him after taking it from inside my bowler hat.

grounded_facts: Holmes uses Watson's stethoscope to detect mechanical sounds beneath the water, indicating artificial origin of the monster.
memories.memory_text: I saw Holmes use my stethoscope to listen beneath the water, and I heard him say, 'I can hear something,' which made me think the sounds were mechanical and not from a living creature.

grounded_facts: The monster passes close to the boat, creating a backwash that rocks it broadside and throws all three occupants into the lake.
memories.memory_text: I saw the monster pass close to our boat, and when I threw the oar at it, the backwash rocked the boat violently and threw me, Holmes, and Gabrielle into the lake.

grounded_facts: The creature is spotted moving through the mist on Loch Ness, approaching the boat before submerging and later resurfacing nearby, causing the boat to capsize.
memories.memory_text: I saw the creature moving through the mist, coming close to our boat before it vanished under the water and then resurfaced nearby; I threw my oar at it, but it knocked us over and I ended up in the lake.

grounded_facts: Watson compares his fear of the monster to past dangers in India, stating he was never half as frightened.
memories.memory_text: I told Holmes and Gabrielle that I've faced man-eating tigers and survived a wild elephant stampede in India, but I wasn't half as frightened then as I was by this creature—it seems to have a personal grudge against us.

grounded_facts: Holmes, Watson, and Gabrielle observe Urquhart Castle from a rowboat and attempt to intercept the Loch Ness Monster after spotting it in the lake.
memories.memory_text: I was in the rowboat with Holmes and Gabrielle, watching Urquhart Castle from across the lake when we spotted the monster in the mist; we started rowing to intercept it, though I wasn't sure what we'd do when we got there.

grounded_facts: Holmes explains that the monster likely returned to the castle for 'supper', implying it is mechanical and operated from within the structure.
memories.memory_text: Holmes told me that the monster likely returned to the castle for 'supper,' and from that, I understood he believed it was mechanical and operated from within the structure.

grounded_facts: After the monster disappears, the wooden scaffolding in front of the castle tower rises into the air, then descends again, suggesting a hidden mechanism connected to the monster.

grounded_facts: Holmes and Watson return to their residence at 221B Baker Street after a journey, greeted by Mrs. Hudson.
Holmes and Watson arrive at 221B Baker Street by hansom cab, marking the beginning of their residence there.
Mrs. Hudson warmly greets Holmes and Watson upon their arrival at 221B Baker Street.
memories.memory_text: I arrived at 221B Baker Street by hansom cab with Watson, returning to our residence, and Mrs. Hudson warmly greeted us as we stepped down.

grounded_facts: Holmes and Watson arrive back at 221B Baker Street, reestablishing the familiar setting and routine.
memories.memory_text: I remember arriving back at 221B Baker Street with Watson, resuming our usual routine as he put down his bag and I pulled up the window shades.

grounded_facts: Holmes accuses Watson of romanticizing and exaggerating his character in published stories.
memories.memory_text: I confronted Watson about how he romanticizes me in his stories—I told him he exaggerates my height, my violin skills, and even dresses me in a costume I never wear, and that he's made me seem like a misogynist when I merely distrust the twinkle in a woman's eye.

grounded_facts: Holmes dismisses the case of the missing Tumbling Piccolos, deeming the reward too low and the matter likely trivial.
memories.memory_text: I dismissed the case of the missing Tumbling Piccolos because the circus owner offered me only five pounds — not even a pound per midget — and I concluded he was a stingy man; it seemed obvious the little chaps had simply run off to join another circus.

grounded_facts: Holmes discovers that something crucial is missing from his desk, which he attributes to Mrs. Hudson's cleaning against his orders.
memories.memory_text: I noticed something missing from my desk and realized it was something very crucial, which I blamed on Mrs. Hudson for tidying up against my explicit orders.

grounded_facts: Holmes explains that dust on his desk is part of his document dating system, justifying his anger at her cleaning.
memories.memory_text: I explained to Mrs. Hudson that the dust on my desk is essential to my filing system, because by its thickness I can date any document immediately.

grounded_facts: Watson explains and justifies Holmes's tobacco ash experiment to Mrs. Hudson, who is critical of the smoky conditions.
memories.memory_text: I heard Watson explain to Mrs. Hudson that I was working on a definitive study of tobacco ash, justifying the smoky conditions she objected to.

grounded_facts: Holmes conducts a scientific experiment involving the combustion and analysis of various tobacco products to study their ash residues.
memories.memory_text: I conducted a scientific experiment analyzing the ash from various tobacco products, studying each sample under my microscope to distinguish their unique residues.

grounded_facts: Holmes tells Watson he envies his calm and untroubled mind, contrasting it with his own restless intellect.
memories.memory_text: I told Watson how I envy his calm and untroubled mind, so different from my own restless intellect that rebels against stagnation like a racing engine tearing itself apart without work, and though he questioned my self-control, I assured him this will take care of it.

grounded_facts: Watson challenges Holmes's decision to use cocaine, questioning his self-control and expressing shame.
memories.memory_text: I heard Watson confront me, asking where my self-control was and if I wasn't ashamed of myself, and though I admitted I was thoroughly ashamed, I told him the injection would take care of it.

grounded_facts: Holmes, feeling mentally stagnant and unchallenged, decides to inject himself with cocaine as a means of coping with his inner restlessness.
memories.memory_text: I felt my mind stagnating, unchallenged and restless, so I decided to inject cocaine to cope with the inner turmoil, taking the bottle from Watson's bag and preparing the syringe in my bedroom.

grounded_facts: Watson claims Holmes only lives with him to access stimulants, challenging the integrity of their relationship.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Watson that the only reason I live with him is to have a steady supply of stimulants.

grounded_facts: Upon Mrs. Hudson's entrance, Holmes conceals the hypodermic syringe behind his back, indicating shame or desire to hide his drug use.
memories.memory_text: I quickly hid the hypodermic syringe behind my back when Mrs. Hudson walked in, not wanting her to see it.

grounded_facts: Holmes tells Watson where he hid his medical bag, demonstrating familiarity and observation.
memories.memory_text: I told Watson his medical bag was under the Moorish table, and I saw him lift the table to retrieve it.

grounded_facts: Watson announces his decision to leave 221B Baker Street and resume his medical practice, marking a significant shift in his living arrangement and relationship with Holmes.
memories.memory_text: I heard Watson announce he is moving out of 221B Baker Street and that he will continue to pay his half of the rent until I find someone else to share the rooms.

grounded_facts: Watson provides Holmes with a new hypodermic needle and leaves behind three bottles of narcotics, symbolizing both care and resignation regarding Holmes's addiction.
memories.memory_text: I saw Watson take a fresh hypodermic needle from his bag and give it to me, followed by placing three bottles of narcotics on the mantel as his farewell gesture.

grounded_facts: Watson states he won't watch Holmes destroy himself with drugs, asserting personal boundaries.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Watson that he won’t watch me destroy myself with drugs, and that if I choose to do so, he’ll leave me to it.

grounded_facts: A heated argument between Watson and Holmes about Holmes's drug use and living situation, culminating in Watson's announcement to move out.
memories.memory_text: I remember the heated argument with Watson about my drug use, during which I tried to return to the living room with my hypodermic, hid it when Mrs. Hudson entered, and later watched him leave after he gave me a fresh needle and said goodbye.

grounded_facts: A structured moment in which Watson packs and prepares to leave 221B Baker Street, marking a significant personal and narrative transition.
Watson begins packing his belongings, indicating his intention to move out of the shared residence with Holmes.
memories.memory_text: I saw Watson moving around the room, collecting his things and packing them into open valises on the bed, clearly preparing to leave 221B Baker Street.

grounded_facts: Watson dismisses Mrs. Hudson's emotional display, signaling his determination to move on.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Watson himself when he dismissed Mrs. Hudson’s sorrow, telling her not to make a scene.

grounded_facts: Watson informs Mrs. Hudson of his temporary lodging at Brown's Hotel.
memories.memory_text: I learned from Watson that he would be staying temporarily at Brown's Hotel after leaving Baker Street.

grounded_facts: Mrs. Hudson expresses sorrow over Watson's departure and references her own past emotional trauma.
memories.memory_text: I heard Mrs. Hudson tell Watson how sad she felt about his departure, saying it reminded her of her own divorce.

grounded_facts: Watson articulates his relief and anticipation about leaving behind the unpredictable and dangerous life with Holmes.
memories.memory_text: I heard Watson say he was actually looking forward to leaving, expressing relief at the idea of returning to a normal life with regular hours and predictable medical emergencies.

grounded_facts: Holmes waves off Mrs. Hudson's complaint about gunshots in the apartment, showing disregard for her authority.
memories.memory_text: I waved off Mrs. Hudson's complaints about the gunshots, telling her she was in my line of fire, and ignored her outrage over the damage I'd made.

grounded_facts: Watson calms Mrs. Hudson by offering to clean the mess and return her belongings.
memories.memory_text: I saw Watson calm Mrs. Hudson by offering to clean up the mess and return her belongings while she unpacked his things.

grounded_facts: Holmes verbally acknowledges his deep, albeit reserved, affection for Watson, marking a rare emotional disclosure.
memories.memory_text: I admitted to Watson that I'm often cold and unemotional, but I told him that, in my own way, I'm very fond of him.

grounded_facts: Holmes tells Watson he would do anything to keep him around, affirming their bond.
memories.memory_text: I told Watson there's nothing I wouldn't do to keep him around, because I meant it—he's essential to me.

grounded_facts: Watson returns to Holmes's residence, possibly considering leaving due to Holmes's drug use, prompting a dramatic performance to retain him.
memories.memory_text: I saw Watson hesitate at the door, and when he said he thought I wouldn't try to stop him from leaving, I told him there's nothing I wouldn't do to keep him here.

grounded_facts: Holmes uses a revolver to smash three bottles he presents as narcotics, but they are later revealed to be substitutes from his chemistry set, part of a performance to convince Watson of his recovery.
memories.memory_text: I used my revolver to smash three bottles I presented as narcotics, knowing they were only substitutes from my chemistry set, and later I placed my violin back among the real bottles hidden in the case.

grounded_facts: Holmes secretly retrieves the real narcotics bottles from the violin case, revealing that the destroyed ones were fakes, indicating his continued dependency.
memories.memory_text: I retrieved the real narcotics bottles from my violin case after making sure Watson was busy, knowing the ones I destroyed were just substitutes from my chemistry set.

grounded_facts: Holmes rejects attending the final performance of the Imperial Russian Ballet despite receiving anonymous tickets and a plea for help.
memories.memory_text: I rejected attending the ballet after receiving anonymous tickets because I suspected it was some sort of plot, and frankly, I detest ballet—it would bore me to death.

grounded_facts: Watson urges Holmes to accept the invitation to the ballet, emphasizing its importance and rarity, but Holmes resists.
memories.memory_text: I remember Watson urging me to go, emphasizing how rare and important the performance was, but I stood my ground.

grounded_facts: The final performance of the Imperial Russian Ballet, specifically Swan Lake, for which tickets are highly sought after.
memories.memory_text: I was told it's the final performance of the Imperial Russian Ballet, Swan Lake, and that the house has been sold out for months.

grounded_facts: Watson reveals that twelve men have died due to their obsession with Petrova, providing background on her dangerous allure.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Watson that twelve men have died for love of Petrova, which he shared with me as part of her dangerous allure.

grounded_facts: Rogozhin abruptly asks Holmes about family medical history, creating tension and suspicion.
memories.memory_text: I was startled when Rogozhin abruptly questioned me about my health and family medical history, and I demanded to know what it was all about, sensing immediate tension.

grounded_facts: A live performance of Swan Lake at the theatre, attended by Holmes and Watson in evening dress.
memories.memory_text: I attended the Swan Lake performance with Watson, sitting in a box while he used his opera glasses and I watched the stage with mild disinterest, noting the pas-de-deux and the audience's applause.
