memories.memory_text: I recognized the woman outside saying 'Auf Wiedersehn' and translated it in the moment, sensing its ironic weight.

grounded_facts: Holmes tells Watson the meaning of the German phrase spoken by the woman outside.
memories.memory_text: I told Watson the meaning of the German phrase the woman outside had said.

grounded_facts: Watson mishears and reacts with annoyance to the German phrase 'Auf Wiedersehn', interpreting it as a sign of arrogance.
memories.memory_text: I saw that Watson misheard the phrase and reacted with annoyance, taking it as a sign of arrogance.

grounded_facts: Watson uses tongs to covertly turn and read the letter from Mycroft after Holmes sets it down.
memories.memory_text: I noticed Watson covertly turning the letter with tongs to read it after I set it down.

grounded_facts: Holmes reads a letter from Mycroft informing him that Ilse von Hoffmanstal was arrested and executed in Japan for espionage.
memories.memory_text: I read the letter from Mycroft and learned that Ilse von Hoffmanstal had been arrested and executed in Japan for espionage.

grounded_facts: After reading the letter, Holmes quietly asks Watson where the file on Ilse von Hoffmanstal is located.

memories.memory_text: My photograph is inside the back of a pocket watch in Watson's dispatch box.
I remember the cold—the water, the blanket, my dress clinging to me—and holding something in my hand, a piece of cardboard with an address, though I don’t know why I had it or how I got there.
I remember hearing the word 'Bruxelles' and something in me hesitated — yes, I think I said it back, 'Je pense que oui,' like a whisper from far away.
I couldn't remember my name when Holmes asked. I tried, but it was gone. I didn't even know who I was.
I woke up when the door clicked shut—someone had been watching me. I thought it was Emile, but my voice trembled as I called out, not knowing who was really there.
I stepped into the room and saw him in the shadows, and I thought it was Emile—I called out to him, rushed to him, held on tight, wanting to feel safe again after all those lonely nights.
He took my hand, held it to the light, and raised a mirror to my palm. I saw the reflection—numbers in green ink, '301', clear in the glass.
I remember stepping down into the shop, the air thick with dust and the sound of birds suddenly flapping—so many canaries under that tarp, I hadn’t expected life in a place that felt so empty.
It struck me then—this dusty, hidden room was the place I’d been writing to all those months, and the thought made my chest tighten, though I didn’t say it right away.
I later learned Watson was apprehensive about me, and Holmes told him I was safe with Mrs. Hudson.
I stood in the doorway, waiting for them to come up the stairs — when I saw Holmes, I had to know, I couldn't hold it in any longer: 'Any news? Did you find out anything?'
I told Holmes I wouldn't go back to Brussels — that I'd keep looking for my husband even if they tried to kill me. My voice was shaking, but I meant every word.
After he explained the plan, I kissed his cheek and thanked him — but later, I had to ask Watson, 'You don't like me very much, do you?' I wasn't sure why, but it mattered to me.
I asked Mr. Holmes if I was embarrassing him, my voice quiet under the covers, and when he said no, I only managed an 'Oh?'—unsure what else to say, my face warm in the dim light.

I remember saying women are never to be trusted, and then realizing he agreed — that he wasn't fond of them either, just like me. It felt like the first time someone truly understood that quiet suspicion I've always carried.

When he told me about his fiancée dying just before their wedding — how he still blamed her unreliability — I didn't know what to say. I only managed 'I'm sorry,' but inside, I felt the weight of how grief had hardened him.
I saw the two small coffins and thought they must be for children — it made me say, 'It's so sad,' because the idea of burying young ones struck me deeply.

Later, hearing the grave-digger speak of a father and two sons found in the loch, I realized the small coffins weren't for children — they were for midgets, though no one said it outright, and that changed the weight of what I'd seen.
I saw his face—Emile’s face—and the ring on his finger, just like mine. I knew it was him, finally.
There was something wrong—his ring was green, and at his feet... white birds, dead. I couldn’t breathe. I must have fallen.

I stepped out of the carriage beside Holmes, the cold morning air sharp against my skin, and watched him sign 'Mr. and Mrs. Ashdown' in the register—my breath caught, realizing I was no longer just a witness, but part of the lie.

I remember taking off my wedding ring, my hands shaking as I handed it to Holmes, and then seeing my husband's ring with that strange green tint—he said it proved Henri didn't drown, and I couldn't stop the tears even when he told me to.
I stood at the window behind Holmes and Watson, watching them react to something on the lake, though I couldn’t see it myself.
I remember the word 'asphyxiation'—it hung in the air when Mr. Holmes said it, and I repeated it quietly, trying to understand what it meant for my husband.
I saw something moving in the mist—something long and dark cutting through the water—and I couldn't speak, only point and scream.
I remember leaving my parasol behind—it was with Watson’s stethoscope on the table in the tent, though I don’t know how it got there. Everything feels unclear, like I wasn’t even there.
I remember waking up when the parasol hit the lampshade—he startled me on purpose. When he asked about the German phrase, I didn’t want to say it, but I knew he’d already won.
I looked at him and said my name clearly—'It's von Hoffmanstal'—feeling something shift inside me, as if I were finally stepping into a role I had been avoiding.
I asked Holmes if I ever fooled him, then said I failed miserably, after he told me my mission was over and Mycroft would take me into custody.
I heard Mycroft say I wasn't going to jail — I was being sent back to Germany, exchanged for one of their agents. I remember feeling stunned, not knowing whether to feel relief or suspicion.

Mycroft said I was better than most British operatives, and Holmes gave me a small bow — I saw it, even though he still wouldn't look me in the eye. I wasn't just being released; I was being acknowledged.
I kept opening and closing my parasol as the carriage pulled away, hoping the signals were clear—Mycroft didn’t seem to notice, but I couldn’t be sure.

memories.memory_text: I was pulling up the window shades when Watson handed me the Strand Magazine with that absurd illustration of me in a deerstalker and Inverness cape—ridiculous costume, entirely my own, yet presented as definitive.
I picked up a dagger and began opening my mail on the dining table.

I remember the weight of the Stradivarius being placed into my hands, offered silently from behind the screen—Petrova’s voice warm with reverence as she called it a gift for the man who solved the Baskerville mystery.

I recall the moment her hand extended in the candlelight—cool, deliberate—and I took it, the gesture feeling less like greeting and more like the sealing of some unspoken bargain, though the true nature of her request had not yet been spoken.

I watched Watson tear apart the smoking machine, his face twisted with outrage, and I offered him an apology laced with absurdity—cornered by a madwoman, I said—knowing full well it would only stoke his panic.
When he stammered that marriage might solve it, I couldn’t help but murmur that they’d really talk—just to watch him recoil, then double down on defiance, as if courage could erase the absurdity.
I examined the soggy cardboard and noticed the faint green ink on the back—once wet, it had smeared, but enough remained to make out 'Bazaar Modern, Bruxelles' beneath the water damage.
I asked if she could recall her own name, and after a pause, she did not answer, so I used other evidence to determine it was Gabrielle.
I stepped into shadow when Gabrielle called out, and she rushed toward me, embracing tightly—her voice trembling as she whispered of nights apart and a pink negligee bought in Brussels.

As she beckoned me to the bed, I saw faint marks on her palm—green ink smudges like those on the cardboard; holding the shaving mirror to her hand, the reflection revealed '301' in reverse, matching the coded message exactly.
I entered the study and saw Mycroft at the refectory table, decanting wine with careful precision. He did not turn to face me as I asked about his health.
He brought us the glasses without mention of the case—only civilities—and I noticed the corner of a telegram visible as he moved, then out of sight as he turned.
I recalled that 'Glennahurich' breaks down into 'glen,' 'na,' and 'hurich'—valley, of the, yew tree—so the boxes were clearly bound for the Valley of the Yew Tree.
As Watson opened the door, a revolver appeared through the gap; I spoke calmly, knowing a sudden move might provoke a shot, and told Mrs. Hudson she’d lose two tenants if she fired.
I told Gabrielle about the woman I once loved who was a murderess—how we had those secret meetings in my laboratory, and all the while she was stealing cyanide to poison her husband.
I recalled my fiancée—daughter of my violin teacher—how we were days from our wedding, invitations sent, tail-coat being fitted, and then she died suddenly of influenza.
I saw the wedding ring on Valladon’s finger had turned green—copper reacting with some corrosive agent, though the nature of it wasn’t immediately clear.
At the foot of the coffin, three canaries lay dead, their feathers bleached a lifeless grey-white.

I compared the greenish tinge on Valladon's copper ring with Gabrielle's, and the difference in corrosion confirmed he hadn't been in the water—drowning was impossible, the cause of death had to be poisoning.
I held up the wedding rings and noted the green corrosion—only chlorine gas could cause that and bleach the color from canaries. That was the key: Valladon didn’t drown, he asphyxiated.

After dismissing Watson’s sighting as imagination, I picked up the guidebook and pointed to the map—our only real lead was the castle reference. The question wasn’t whether there was a castle, but which one.
I turned the tandem around without a word—when denied at the front, the logical path is always the back way.
I corrected the guide’s mistake—1400 and James the Third was wrong; it’s 1500 and James the Fourth. A proper guide shouldn’t miss that by a century and a king.
I heard the chirping—those weren’t ordinary birds. When I saw the cage from Ashdown Street and the crate marked 'Sulphuric Acid,' I knew something was hidden here.
I saw the creature's neck break the water through the mist, grabbed Watson's arm to pull him back when he stood, then said 'Quick, Watson. After it!' and took up my oar to row toward it.
After the wake faded and the creature submerged, I stopped rowing and said we'd lost it—then hushed Watson, straining to hear any sound beneath the water, though only the lap of waves answered.

I paced the room, whistling 'Swan Lake,' and realized the creature in the lake was no beast, but a machine—an artificial heart, lungs powered by an air pump, bubbles betraying its mechanism. The stethoscope had confirmed it: metal, not muscle.

The hotel manager brought a magnum of champagne for 'Mr. Ashdown' and told me to deliver it, though I hadn't ordered it. He knew my real name. A carriage waited downstairs. I tapped the bottle and said the last act was beginning.
I climbed into the gig with the guide, champagne bottle in hand, and asked who was minding the castle—only to be told to get on, as it was late.
I stepped onto the red carpet铺 across the courtyard, noting how freshly unrolled it was—torch-lit, precise—and remarked on the unnecessary gesture, only for Mycroft to dismiss it as not meant for me.
I handed Mycroft the champagne, dryly noting its poor quality, and watched as he passed it to a black-suited man who took it wordlessly toward the tower.
I saw the name E. Valladon on the trunk and paused. Gabrielle's parasol and Watson's stethoscope were on the table among engineering models.

I deduced the craft used sulphuric acid batteries and canaries to detect gas—details too specific to be coincidence. But Mycroft’s silence after my explanation made me realize I’d been feeding insights to the wrong side.
I was standing among the scientists when the Queen noticed me and asked about my contribution—her attention was unexpected, and I downplayed my role as usual.

After Mycroft introduced me as his brother, the Queen acknowledged she knew my name and had been following my exploits—then asked if Watson would publish the story, as though I were a figure of public interest.

I swung the parasol to strike the lampshade, startling Gabrielle awake—her reaction confirmed she was no longer playing the part of the innocent. When I pressed her on the German phrase, she hesitated just long enough to betray her knowledge: 'Unter dem Schloss.'

relations.relation_summary: Holmes and Watson share a multifaceted relationship defined by deep professional collaboration and personal companionship. Social relationship evidence consistently labels them as collaborators, colleagues, and companions, with repeated references to their joint investigations, shared living arrangements at 221B Baker Street, and long-term cohabitation as 'bachelors' for five years. Their partnership is characterized by mutual reliance: Holmes frequently consults Watson on medical and observational matters, trusts him with sensitive tools like his stethoscope, and values his presence enough to declare he would do anything to retain him. Watson, in turn, supports Holmes emotionally and professionally, documenting his cases for publication and expressing concern over Holmes' cocaine use, which reveals both care and disapproval. This emotional duality surfaces in recurring conflicts—Holmes dismisses social norms and ethical concerns, while Watson challenges him on professional ethics, drug use, and deceptive actions, such as when he accuses Holmes of lacking decency or expresses anger over reputational risks. Despite these tensions, Holmes offers apologies for misunderstandings, and Watson remains loyal, indicating resilience in their bond. Key shared events reinforce this dynamic: they investigate cases together—from examining clues in suitcases to bicycling toward leads—coordinate entry through tradesmen’s entrances, observe funerals from hiding, and jointly interact with clients like Gabrielle and Madame Valladon. Moments of intimacy, such as Watson nudging Holmes while dozing or Holmes requesting simple items like a butter-knife, underscore domestic familiarity. Holmes’ admiration for Watson’s mind and Watson’s self-identification as both 'friend' and 'valet' reflect a blend of personal affection and professional duty. The relationship evolves through conflict and reconciliation, maintaining a stable core of trust and interdependence that shapes their decisions—Watson repeatedly follows Holmes into danger, and Holmes adjusts his behavior in response to Watson’s moral feedback. While some external characters imply a romantic dimension, the evidence supports a deeply affectionate but primarily platonic partnership rooted in intellectual synergy and emotional loyalty.

The relationship between Holmes and Madame is defined by a pragmatic and transactional collaboration centered on the conception of a child, suggesting a calculated arrangement rather than an emotional or romantic bond. Holmes proposes mutual benefits—Madame would return to St. Petersburg with the child while he returns to London—indicating a planned separation after fulfilling their shared objective, which underscores the instrumental nature of their connection. This collaborative arrangement is further contextualized by Holmes assuming a position of advisory authority when he cautions Madame Petrova against hasty decisions, invoking his identity as an Englishman and cultural stereotypes to justify his perspective. In this interaction, Holmes performs a guiding role while Madame undergoes the influence of his counsel, revealing a power dynamic where Holmes exerts rational control while Madame appears in a more receptive, possibly vulnerable position. The emotional dynamics appear restrained and intellectualized, with no evidence of intimacy or deep personal connection. The relationship does not show signs of evolution within the provided evidence, remaining anchored in practicality and asymmetrical communication. I told Mrs. Hudson to pack my bags and said I was moving out — I could see the surprise on her face, and Holmes pretending he hadn’t seen it coming.

I found my medical bag under the Moorish table, took out a fresh hypodermic needle and three bottles of narcotics, and put them on the mantel. I told Holmes it was my farewell present and that I wouldn't watch him destroy himself.
I would gladly have murdered him — had it not been for my saintly disposition — over his refusal to go to the ballet, even with a desperate plea and free tickets in hand.

I stood in the doorway of his bedroom, holding the letter and tickets, trying to convince him to go. I told him it was the final performance of the Imperial Russian Ballet, sold out for months, with seats at a guinea each. I read the note: 'Please! You are the only man in the world who can help me.'
I stormed into the flat and shouted his name—'Holmes!'—my voice cutting through the quiet, my breath sharp from the climb and the weight of what I was about to say.

I told Holmes we had nothing to hide, that we could sue anyone who started a rumor, and I even tried to lighten it by mentioning women from three continents who'd testify for me — but he didn’t respond, just stood there silent, and I started to worry.

I asked if there had ever been women in his life, hoping I wasn’t overstepping, and when he said 'yes,' I actually felt relief — until he added, 'You're being presumptuous,' and shut the door, leaving me standing there.
I saw the bruise on her temple and the way she was shivering—she was soaked, half-conscious, and in shock. The moment I reached the bottom of the stairs, I knew she needed warmth and care.

I led her to the chair by the fire and felt her cold skin—she was in shock, soaked through and barely responsive, so I began rubbing her wrists to bring back circulation while noting the bruise on her temple.

I saw the coagulated blood on her temple and knew the injury wasn't from a fall—someone had struck her deliberately, so I told Holmes to get my bag, needing proper tools to assess what she'd been through.
I was in excruciating pain from sleeping on that damn couch, and I had to beg Mrs. Hudson to press her knee into my back just below the seventh vertebra until I heard a snap.
I heard Mrs. Hudson say 'She's gone,' and when I saw Gabrielle's bed empty with her clothes still there, I rushed to Holmes' room and shouted that she was gone—then froze at the door.
I handed the hammer and chisel to Holmes after he dropped inside, then I squeezed through the skylight and jumped to the floor.

I stopped Holmes on the steps of the Diogenes Club because I had to admit I was apprehensive—not about Mycroft, but about confronting Madame Valladon.

I pressed Holmes again as we came up the stairs—Mycroft’s orders weren’t just family advice, they represented the government, and I needed to know if he intended to defy them outright.
I agreed to escort Gabrielle to Victoria Station as part of Holmes's plan, though I didn't fully understand his intentions—I only knew she was distressed and needed guidance.
I helped Gabrielle find her missing glove by looking under the couch and gave it back to her.

I adjusted the telescope and saw it—through the mist, something with a long neck moving just beneath the surface of the lake.
I saw it—clear as day—through the telescope. I practically shouted at Holmes to look, thrusting the instrument into his hands, my heart pounding with the certainty that this was real.
I saw it—clear as anything—rising from the lake, no matter what Holmes says; I grabbed the telescope and searched the water, but it was gone.
I stood there, halfway through the French window, and told Holmes he was the least logical man I knew — how could he dismiss what I saw as imagination, after always saying I had none?
I saw it—something huge, a long neck cutting through the mist and water, moving like no natural beast should. I stood up in shock, shouting Holmes’s name before he pulled me back down.
